steps.goal: Publish a minimal, adoptable C++ toolkit with docs and a 3‑minute demo that gets a novice team to a working autonomous in under 90 minutes.
steps.title: Turn your existing VEX code + lessons into VEX FastStart (shippable kit)

importantMoves: Scope FastStart to 3 components: (1) Auton routine selector, (2) PID + odometry template with sane defaults, (3) 6-lesson quickstart you already teach.
Create a clean GitHub repo (MIT license), QuickStart.md, and a 3‑minute demo video showing setup and a basic run.
Write a 1‑page Impact Brief template with two metrics you can capture in pilots: time-to-first-auton, auton points gained in scrimmage.
externalLeverage: VEX Forum and TSA Indiana channels are primed audiences who understand C++/VEX; post only after repo is live.
Project Next Vision clients as first adopters for fast feedback.
completionSignals: Public GitHub repo with docs and demo video link.
Impact Brief template ready to send to testers.

steps.goal: Get 8–12 students (3–5 teams) to install and run FastStart, capturing before/after metrics and 3 testimonials.
steps.title: Seed adoption and collect proof with a 2-hour ‘Auton Saturday’ mini-workshop
steps.asymmetricMove: Use CSO/TSA lists and your tutoring clients to fill the room in days; you already have the space, trust, and cadence to run it smoothly.
importantMoves: Invite list: CSO members, TSA chapter teams, your 10+ tutoring clients; cap at ~12 students for hands-on success.
Run a tight agenda: 20‑min overview, 60‑min guided build, 20‑min scrimmage to measure auton points, 20‑min feedback + quotes.
Collect metrics and short quotes on paper or a Google Form; secure permission to use team names in the repo README.
externalLeverage: TSA advisor to reserve robotics room and vouch for attendance.
ZCHS announcements/CSO newsletter for targeted RSVPs (not public blasting).
completionSignals: At least 3 teams complete a working auton with FastStart during the session.
You have 2–3 quantified before/after metrics and 3+ testimonial quotes.

steps.goal: Ship a crisp public package: updated README with metrics, a 90‑second demo cut, and a short reflection tying engineering choices to systems thinking.
steps.title: Make the proof legible for admissions and teams
steps.asymmetricMove: Your debate background lets you write a tight reflection that reads like uncommon judgment for a HS engineer.
importantMoves: Update README with adoption numbers, team names (with consent), and quotes; add an Impact section up top.
Publish a 90‑second demo cut focused on outcomes (first auton in 53 minutes; +10 auton points in scrimmage).
Write a 600–800 word reflection: what PID/odometry tradeoffs you made, how you teach them, and how that mirrors decisions in larger systems.
externalLeverage: VEX Forum post linking to repo after testimonials are in; ask for 1–2 code reviews from known coaches/upperclassmen for polish.
completionSignals: Repo shows metrics and testimonials; demo video is live and linked.
Reflection is published (repo docs or personal site) and ready to cite in essays.

steps.goal: Secure letters that describe your initiative and user impact, not just talent.
steps.title: Lock recommenders and aim their letters at what you just proved
steps.asymmetricMove: Give your TSA advisor and VEX coach a one-page Impact Brief so they can cite concrete adoption and leadership they witnessed.

Ask counselor to mention $20k fund stewardship + event ops paired with technical leadership.

externalLeverage: Dana Whitfield or Marcus Reyes for a short outside note only if your ED school permits additional recommendations or Additional Info quotes.
ZCHS counseling office to clarify caps on external letters.
completionSignals: Recommenders confirm receipt of materials and deadlines; outside endorser drafted (if allowed).
At least one recommender references FastStart impact in a preview or email acknowledgement.

steps.goal: Finish Common App personal statement and ED supplements that anchor on FastStart + outreach, with live links.
steps.title: Write ED essays that point to real links and decisions you own

Draft ED supplements that reference the repo, demo, and reflection; include 1–2 sentences on why the school’s labs/clubs map to expanding FastStart (do not promise new products).
Have Priya mark what reads generic; fix with concrete nouns (team names, metrics, file names) and remove buzzwords.
QA links (GitHub, video) and file naming; export a clean PDF of the Impact Brief for counselor/Additional Info if space permits.
externalLeverage: Priya Raman for school-specific tone and prompts.
School writing center or trusted English teacher for line edits without sanding off your technical specificity.
completionSignals: Essays hit word counts, include 1–2 live links, and survive two external reads (Priya + one teacher).
All supplements are finalized in your ED portal drafts.

steps.goal: ED application submitted 3–10 days before deadline; light plan to maintain project momentum and send an update only if material.

VEX Forum and CSO newsletter as light-touch distribution to sustain adoption without heavy new builds.

asymmetricThesis: Turn your existing VEX C++ codebase and tutoring curriculum into a public, adoptable toolkit (VEX FastStart) and seed it through CSO/TSA/tutoring for immediate, countable users.
Use Priya Raman (Penn) to shape ED supplements to a single school’s ethos, while your artifact provides the hard evidence those essays point to.

Leverage Dana Whitfield and/or Marcus Reyes for a tightly scoped, one-paragraph endorsement or quote about your initiative (only if your ED school accepts additional recommendations or quotes in Additional Info).
Package Student Council $20k operations into a brief that proves you already manage resources and teams—paired with the toolkit’s rollout, this reads as “builder who ships and scales.”

Use your debate background to publish a concise technical-reflection piece that links engineering decisions in the toolkit (PID/odometry tradeoffs) to systems thinking—unique angle most HS applicants won’t have.
strategicDiagnosis: ED odds improve when your application shows shipped impact and a tight narrative; you have raw fuel (VEX wins, TSA leadership, CSO distribution, tutoring clients) but the proof isn’t yet packaged into a visible, sharable artifact tied to users.

Your warm access to an energy VC (Dana Whitfield) and a grid executive (Marcus Reyes) is rare for a high school applicant; these should be used narrowly (precision endorsements and reality-checks), not as new, heavy projects pre-ED.
You can reach users instantly: 150+ CSO members, TSA/VEX teams, and 10+ tutoring clients. Converting this private reach into public adoption metrics is the fastest path to non-generic impact.

Debate accolades on tech policy are distinctive; they should frame essays as “I turn competitive tech into community infrastructure,” connecting policy judgment to practical tools you built for peers.
Risk right now is time: senior fall. Any plan that starts a net-new startup, new stack, or research track is likely to dilute essay quality and adoption metrics before Nov 1.
